Where it began

Sanath Jayasuriya was born in Matara, in the south of Sri Lanka, on 30 June 1969. He learned the game at St. Servatius' College, where he captained the side in its big annual match in 1988, the same year he was named the Observer Schoolboy Cricketer of the Year in the outstation section. That year he also played in the first Under-19 World Cup in Australia. A few months later, on a Sri Lanka B tour of Pakistan, he began his first-class career with two unbeaten double-centuries, which is one way to get noticed.

The player

Jayasuriya played 110 Tests from 1991 to 2007, the first Sri Lankan to reach a hundred of them. He made 6,973 runs at 40.07 with 14 hundreds and 31 fifties, took 98 wickets with his left-arm spin and held 72 catches. He led Sri Lanka in 38 Tests and won 18.

His great Test innings came against India in Colombo in 1997: 340 in 799 minutes, while he and Roshan Mahanama put on 576 for the second wicket, then a record for any partnership in Tests. Sri Lanka finished on 952 for 6. In one-day cricket he was a force of nature. At the 1996 World Cup he and Romesh Kaluwitharana attacked from the very first over, Sri Lanka won the trophy without losing a game, and Jayasuriya was named player of the tournament. Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1997.

What made him special

Before him, openers in one-day cricket mostly eased their way in. Jayasuriya saw the fielding restrictions as an invitation and hit the new ball over the infield, a plan that teams everywhere soon copied. His favourite stroke was a lofted cut over point. Against Pakistan in 1996 he reached a hundred in 48 balls, and against India at Sharjah in 2000 he made 189. With the ball he bowled left-arm spin with a quick arm and a fondness for the faster ball, got through his overs in a hurry, and took 323 one-day wickets, which made him the only cricketer with 10,000 runs and 300 wickets in one format.

If there was a flaw it was that patience never came naturally. Then again, 799 minutes at the crease in Colombo suggests he could find some when the mood took him.

Away from the middle

He kept playing long after most openers stop, scoring a one-day hundred on his 39th birthday at the 2008 Asia Cup and playing for the Mumbai Indians in the first season of the Indian Premier League. He later chaired Sri Lanka's selection panel, a period that took in the 2014 World Twenty20 title, and in 2024 became the national team's head coach.

And finally

In his last Test, at Kandy in 2007, he hit James Anderson for six fours in a single over. Some players slip quietly away. Jayasuriya left the way he had arrived, with the fielders chasing the ball to the boundary.
